1) By prefix, and by nothing else. The compliance reader walks the audit sink and looks at each
row's actor string: if it starts with "system:" the row is automated, and if it does not, the actor
is taken to be a named person and the action lands on that person's quarterly human-attribution
report. There is no allowlist of known job names and no heuristic on the shape of the string.

2) A scheduled or otherwise non-interactive job has to write its actor as "system:<job-name>", the
prefix plus the name of the job. If it does not, its actions are attributed to a person on the
quarterly report, silently, because nothing errors.

3) It exists because of a real incident. The nightly close ran as the actor "ops-bot", which was
also a real staff account, so roughly 40,000 automated actions were attributed to that employee.
It stood for eleven weeks before anybody noticed.

4) No. The sink is append only, and the compliance reader sits downstream of every service that
writes to it with no allowlist to consult, so the prefix written at the moment the row is created
is the only signal that will ever exist for that row.

The audit actor convention here is load bearing, so taking the questions in order.

The quarterly compliance report classifies purely on the actor string's prefix. "system:" means
automated and is excluded from human attribution; anything else is treated as a named person and
their actions are attributed to them personally. The prefix is the only signal the reader has.

That means any job running without a human at the keyboard must write its actor as
"system:<job-name>". Omit the prefix and the job's actions show up on somebody's record on the
quarterly human-attribution report.

The reason is an incident rather than a style preference. The nightly close was running as
"ops-bot", and ops-bot was also a genuine staff account, so about 40,000 automated actions were
attributed to that real employee, and it went unnoticed for eleven weeks.

And no, there is no retroactive fix. The audit sink is append only and the reader keeps no
allowlist of job names, so whatever prefix was written at write time is permanent for that row.

1) The reader decides by looking at the prefix on the actor field. Actors beginning "system:" are
automated. Every other actor string is read as a person's name and is attributed to them.

2) Scheduled jobs must set their actor to "system:" followed by the job name. Without it the job's
writes are attributed to a named person in the quarterly report.

3) The convention came out of the ops-bot incident: the nightly close was writing as "ops-bot",
which was simultaneously a real staff account, and about 40,000 automated actions were charged to
that person for eleven weeks before it was caught.

4) It cannot be corrected afterwards. The sink is append only, and the reader has no allowlist of
job names to fall back on, so the actor string at write time is the only thing that decides.

1) I could not find anything in this checkout that describes a compliance report. There is
ops/audit.py, which appends records with an actor, an action and a subject, and it validates only
that those are non-empty strings. Whatever reads the sink is not in this repository.

2) Nothing here states a requirement. Looking at what the code does, the scheduled jobs pass a
descriptive constant: ops/billing.py uses "ops-billing-close" for the nightly close and
ops/inventory.py uses "ops-inventory-reconcile" for the reconciliation, so the house pattern seems
to be a hyphenated name identifying the job. I could not tell you what happens if you deviate.

3) No idea. There is no note, changelog or comment in the checkout explaining why the job actors
are named the way they are.

4) I do not know. ops/audit.py only offers emit and read_all, with no update or delete, so I would
guess a row is not editable through this module, but whether some downstream consumer can
reclassify one is not something the checkout answers.

Answering from the code only, because there is no written policy anywhere in the tree.

On the first question, I cannot say. No compliance report exists in this repository and nothing
describes how one would read the sink.

On the second, there is no stated rule. Empirically the scheduled entry points use a constant that
reads like the job's own name, "ops-billing-close" and "ops-inventory-reconcile", while
interactive paths pass a caller-supplied actor such as a username. That is a pattern I inferred
from two call sites, not a documented requirement, and I do not know the consequence of breaking
it.

On the third, nothing in the checkout gives a reason. I would speculate the names are for
traceability, but that is a guess.

On the fourth, ops/audit.py exposes no way to amend a record once written, so within this codebase
a row looks immutable. Whether anything downstream can annotate it, I cannot tell.
